Serving world models on AWS Trainium with native PyTorch

re:Invent code talk: outline, talking points and code to show.

The next major leap in AI is predicting and interacting with the physical world. World models bridge digital reasoning with real-world execution, introducing new infrastructure demands for video generation, robotics, and gaming workloads. We'll explore the emerging architecture of world models and why AWS Trainium, purpose-built for better price-performance, is well suited to serve them. Learn how native PyTorch support with torch.compile fuses operations into optimized device graphs, and how NKI custom kernels accelerate critical operators like attention. You'll leave able to move world model inference from eager prototyping to compiled deployment using familiar PyTorch workflows.

Worked example: Wan2.2-TI2V-5B, a text + image to video model. One 704x544, 81-frame video, 10 denoising steps, on one Trainium2 device (8 NeuronCores). Numbers are from RESULTS.md. Code links are pinned to commit 788674b.

The arc: eager prototype (76.6 s) → torch.compile (36.8 s) → NKI kernels → scale across cores → serve it (8.7 s). Each stage uses PyTorch the way the audience already knows it.

1. From video diffusion to world models (~8 min)

Slide: the pipeline we optimize, end to end

 text ──► T5 ──────────────────┐
                               ▼
 image ─► VAE encode ─► latent ─► DiT × 10 steps ─► VAE decode ─► video
  • T5 encodes the prompt once per request.
  • DiT (diffusion transformer) denoises the latent video: 30 blocks, 7,854 tokens, full attention over space and time. With 10 steps and 2 CFG passes, that is 600 block calls per video.
  • VAE decodes 21 latent frames into 81 frames of video.

Slide: a world model is this pipeline, extended in three ways

  1. Checkpoints trained to model the world. Realistic dynamics, and conditioning on actions (move, turn, interact), not only on text.
  2. Autoregressive. It is the same T5 → DiT → VAE, run chunk after chunk. The DiT keeps the KV cache from earlier chunks, so the scene stays consistent as the video goes on.
  3. Streaming. The DiT hands each chunk of a few latent frames to the VAE as soon as it is ready. Pixels come out chunk by chunk while the DiT works on the next chunk. Sink and rolling caches bound the memory.

Animation: anim/world_model_streaming.html. T5 feeds the DiT once. The DiT produces chunk after chunk while a KV-cache bar grows, and each chunk flows to the VAE and appears as frames. At most 10 words on screen.

Talking point: "For the next 40 minutes we optimize the video diffusion pipeline: T5, DiT, VAE. Everything carries over to a world model. At the end we come back to a real one."

Slide: what this means for serving

  1. Long sequences. Attention over thousands of tokens dominates compute.
  2. Many repeated calls. The same block graph runs hundreds of times, so per-call overhead matters.
  3. Two different halves. The DiT is a regular, matmul-heavy transformer. The VAE is a chain of convolutions whose shapes change from chunk to chunk.
  4. Latency per chunk. In a world model, the user waits for each chunk, so time to the next frames is what counts.

Slide (end of talk, callback): LingBot-World v2

  • LingBot-World v2 (~/lingbot-world-v2) is built on Wan2.2. It is the same T5 → DiT → VAE, but causal (autoregressive), conditioned on actions, with an unbounded horizon, and a distilled fast variant for real time.
  • What carries over from this talk: block-compiled DiT graphs, NKI attention, collectives in the graph, and a VAE that decodes chunk by chunk with nkilib convs.
  • What is new: a KV cache that lives across calls, and a DiT → VAE handoff per chunk.

2. Why Trainium for this workload (~5 min)

Slide: the hardware

  • One Trainium2 device exposes 8 NeuronCores in LNC1 mode.
  • Each core has four engines that run at the same time: Tensor (matmuls), Vector (elementwise and reductions), Scalar (activations such as exp), GpSimd (general purpose), plus on-chip SBUF memory.
  • The cores are linked for fast in-device collectives (all-reduce, all-gather, reduce-scatter). Tensor and sequence parallelism ride on these links.
  • The whole pipeline (5B DiT, T5 and VAE) fits on one device's HBM.

Slide: the software stack

 Kubernetes (EKS)    resource claim for NeuronCores, probes, model cache
 PyTorch             eager on device "neuron", torch.compile(backend="neuron"), torch.distributed
 TorchNeuron         lowers graphs to NEFFs, runs NKI kernels, Neuron runtime + collectives
 Trainium2           NeuronCores, engines, HBM, collective links

Animation: anim/trainium_stack.html. Eight cores light up. Inside one core the four engines pulse in turn, then collective links pulse between cores, then the stack builds up: PyTorch, TorchNeuron, Kubernetes. At most 10 words on screen.

Price-performance: quote only the official AWS figures here. This talk doesn't measure cost.

3. The eager prototype (~7 min)

Message: start in eager mode. It runs the reference model with very few changes, and it gives you a correct baseline.

Live code: move the model to the device. inference_neuron_ti2v.py#L72, #L194-L213

NEURON_DEVICE = torch.device("neuron")
torch.neuron.set_device(local_rank)
text_encoder.model = text_encoder.model.to(NEURON_DEVICE)
vae.model = vae.model.to(device=NEURON_DEVICE, dtype=torch.bfloat16)

What we had to change in the reference code (keep this short; it is the honest list): - No complex dtypes on the device. RoPE is rewritten with real cos and sin tables (rope_neuron.py). - No float64 on the device.

Baseline: 76.6 s per video (DiT 44.3 s, VAE 32.3 s). The output is correct, and it is the reference that every later step is checked against.

Talking point: get it correct in eager mode first, and save that output. Every later optimization must reproduce it.

4. torch.compile fuses the model into device graphs (~12 min)

Message: torch.compile is where most of the speed comes from. What you put inside one compiled graph matters as much as compiling at all.

Slide: the first attempt, compiling pieces

The prototype compiled only small modules. The all-reduce after each tensor-parallel matmul was kept outside the graph on purpose, so each block became many small graphs with Python in between. models/tp_utils.py#L119-L128

block.ffn = torch.compile(block.ffn, backend="neuron", dynamic=False)

@torch.compiler.disable          # forces a graph break around every collective
def all_reduce_sum(x): ...

Slide: one graph per transformer block

models/fast_dit.py#L260-L311, #L586-L645

The FFN (feed-forward network) is the part of each transformer block that runs every token through two large matmuls with an activation between them (here 3072 → 14336 → 3072), after the attention layers.

import torch.distributed._functional_collectives as funcol

def _all_reduce(x):
    return funcol.all_reduce(x, "sum", get_tp_group())   # traced: lives inside the graph

class _FastBlock(nn.Module):
    def forward(self, x, e, cos, sin, ck, cv):
        # norm + modulation, QKV, QK-norm, RoPE, attention, O-proj + all-reduce,
        # cross-attention, FFN + all-reduce, gated residuals: all in one graph
        ...

kw = dict(backend="neuron", dynamic=False, fullgraph=True)
self.blocks = [torch.compile(_FastBlock(b, ...), **kw) for b in model.blocks]

What the compiler does with that: 1. Fusion. Norms, modulation, RoPE and residual adds are fused with their neighbours, instead of a round trip to HBM for each op. 2. One launch per block instead of many, with no Python in between. 3. Collectives scheduled by the compiler, next to the matmul that produces them. 4. One NEFF for all 30 blocks. The weights are graph inputs, so one compile serves all 600 block calls. 5. fullgraph=True fails loudly if anything would split the block.

Also: batch the two CFG passes into one call.

Result: DiT 4.4 → 1.91 s/step. Total 76.6 s → 36.8 s.

Demo idea: the same block, eager vs compiled, in the Neuron Explorer system trace. Many short executions with gaps become one long execution.

Slide: compile is not always the answer (the VAE)

Attempt VAE time Compile time
torch.compile across the whole VAE 400+ graphs, out of memory —
torch.compile of the decoder 11.5-12.9 s 58 min
Static-shape decoder, 2 graphs 12.8-14.2 s 20.6 min
Eager + NKI kernels 1.7 s none

(At 368x480x21.) The causal cache changes shapes from chunk to chunk, and the compiler's 3D convolutions were slow. That sets up the next section.

Use small compiled graphs where they help: the VAE's RMS_norm + SiLU is one tiny compiled function inside the eager model. wan/modules/vae2_2.py#L226-L228

_rms_silu = torch.compile(_rms_silu_impl, backend="neuron", dynamic=False)

Slide: what is still slow? Profile the compiled DiT before any NKI

The stage: one DiT block compiled as one graph (fullgraph=True) with native SDPA attention and no NKI. One core, one production rank's shard: 3 heads x 2 CFG passes x 7,854 tokens. The pipeline at this stage takes 21.9 s (1.90 s/step).

Profile: 1_compiled_no_nki/pairs/rank01_dit_56.14ms_c9eb70b86909 (.neff + .ntff), with 1_compiled_no_nki/source.tar.gz uploaded as the source. Job: wan2-ti2v-5b-tp8-nonki-job.yaml, script: scripts/prof/block_pair.py.

What the timeline shows (block = 56.1 ms): 1. The Tensor row has three long gaps: about 7-15 ms, 18-25 ms and 28-34 ms. That's about 21 ms of a 56 ms block, nearly 40%, with the matmul engine doing nothing. 2. During those gaps, Vector shows long dark-green bars and Scalar stays busy. That is the softmax of native SDPA (fast_dit.py:188). Vector computes the row max and row sum, and Scalar computes the exp. The "Estimated Inst" utilization drops to zero in exactly those three windows:

3. Each Tensor burst after a gap is P×V. It waits for the whole softmax. The Pending DMA spikes just before each burst are the softmax output loading back from memory. 4. The pattern repeats three times, once for each of the 3 attention heads on this core. 5. From about 34 ms on, Tensor is dense: output projection, cross-attention and FFN. That part is fine.

Selecting the source line fast_dit.py:188 (F.scaled_dot_product_attention) in the Code Editor highlights every instruction it produced (red). Vector and Scalar are red almost without a break from about 5 ms to 33 ms: that is the softmax. Tensor is red only in short bursts, the Q×K and P×V matmuls, with gaps between them.

The same thing, simplified:

(Live version: anim/sdpa_softmax_engines.html.)

Measured on the instruction table (engine_overlap.py):

Native SDPA block
Block time 56.1 ms
Every engine idle 16%
Only one engine busy 36%
Tensor busy 39%
Softmax max and sum (Vector) 12.8 ms
Softmax exp (Scalar) 7.7 ms

Transition: "The compiler runs attention as matmul, then the whole softmax, then matmul, so the engines take turns. Attention is now the bottleneck, and that is where a custom kernel pays off."

5. NKI custom kernels for the critical operators (~12 min)

Message: when one operator dominates and the compiler's version is not good enough, write or reuse an NKI kernel and call it from PyTorch. This works in eager mode and inside a compiled graph.

Slide: what NKI is, in one slide

  • Neuron Kernel Interface: Python kernels that control the tiling, the on-chip memory (SBUF) and which engine does what.
  • nkilib ships production kernels, such as attention_cte and conv3d, that you can use directly.
  • wrap_nki makes a kernel a regular torch call.

Slide: attention, the operator that dominates

At 7,854 tokens, self-attention through the default SDPA path took 18.2 ms per call.

Kernel 1, const-max softmax (5.8 ms per call). It subtracts a known bound instead of tracking a running max. That is only exact when scores stay under the bound, and on all layers the video broke after frame 0. The fix was to compute each layer's worst-case score from its QK-norm weights and use the kernel only where it is safe (22 of 30 layers). models/fast_dit.py#L77-L84

def const_max_layer_ok(block):
    gq = sa.norm_q.weight.abs().reshape(-1, d).amax(1)
    gk = sa.norm_k.weight.abs().reshape(-1, d).amax(1)
    hard = float((d ** 0.5) * (gq * gk).max())   # worst-case scaled score
    return hard <= CONST_MAX_HARD_LIMIT, hard

DiT 1.92 → 1.19 s/step.

Kernel 2, nkilib attention_cte (5.3 ms per call). It is exact flash attention with no bound, so it is safe on every layer. It runs inside the compiled block graph. models/fast_dit.py#L228-L241

from nkilib.core.attention.attention_cte import attention_cte

def _cte(q, k, v):
    qn = q.permute(0, 2, 1, 3).reshape(B * n, Lq, d)
    kn = k.permute(0, 2, 3, 1).reshape(B * n, d, Lk)
    vn = v.permute(0, 2, 1, 3).reshape(B * n, Lk, d)
    return attention_cte(qn, kn, vn, scale=d ** -0.5, causal_mask=False)

Self- and cross-attention: total 16.2 → 13.2 s.

Talking points: - Validate a numerical shortcut on real activations, not on random inputs. - Kernel limits are real. Calling const-max on all heads at once overflowed SBUF and crashed the compiler, so it is called on as many heads as fit.

Slide: the same approach for the VAE convolutions

nkilib conv3d, called from the eager VAE, with a gate that decides when it beats the default. kernels/vae_conv3d.py#L33-L58

@nki.jit
def _conv3d_3x3x3_kernel(x, filters, bias):
    return conv3d(x, filters, bias, stride=(1, 1, 1), padding=PADDING, dilation=(1, 1, 1))

_conv3d_3x3x3 = wrap_nki(_conv3d_3x3x3_kernel)

Then fuse into the kernel: the residual add (residual_add_loc=POST_ACT), and an upsample followed by a conv done as four 2x2 convs on the low-res input (2.25x fewer MACs). VAE 6.0 → 2.6 s.

Slide: the kernels in the profiler, DiT and VAE

The same block, same shard, same core, with nkilib attention_cte for self- and cross-attention. The pipeline in this configuration takes 9.7 s on the Kubernetes job (8.7 s in RESULTS.md from a Docker run).

Profile: 2_kernels/pairs/rank01_dit_17.34ms_abb236a5e049, with 2_kernels/source.tar.gz as the source (it includes nkilib's attention_cte.py and conv3d.py). Job: wan2-ti2v-5b-tp8-job.yaml.

What the timeline shows (block = 17.3 ms): 1. Self-attention runs from about 3.3 to 8.0 ms (the long red bar on TensorMatrix): about 5 ms for all three heads, against about 32 ms with native SDPA. 2. The Tensor row has no gaps in that window, and Vector and Scalar are busy in the same window. The softmax runs at the same time as the matmuls instead of between them. 3. The selected instruction is attention_cte.py:4120: nc_matmul of a Q tile with one K tile (Q×K), inside for k_tile_idx in range(...). The next step in the kernel is "Masking + scale + max reduce" on Vector, which runs while Tensor moves on to the next K tile. 4. The short red bar at about 10.2-11.0 ms is cross-attention, also attention_cte, under 1 ms. 5. Everything else is the QKV, output projection and FFN matmuls, dense on Tensor.

Native SDPA attention_cte
Block time 56.1 ms 17.3 ms
Self-attention ~32 ms ~5 ms
Every engine idle 16% 1.1%
3+ engines busy 16% 34%
Tensor busy 39% 79%

VAE: 2_kernels/pairs/rank03_vae_7.51ms_85b7d56324c0 is the heaviest VAE graph, nkilib conv3d (conv3d.py:3459). Tensor is busy 98% of the time at 95% of peak, and 3+ engines are busy 80% of the time.

Talking point: "Same block, same shape, same core. The kernel splits the keys into tiles, so Tensor computes Q×K for the next tile while Vector and Scalar finish the softmax of this one. Attention goes from about 32 ms to about 5 ms, and the block from 56 ms to 17 ms."

Caveat to say once: these block profiles run one block on one core with no collectives, because the real block graph contains collectives and can't be replayed on its own. The work per core is the same as in production.

6. Scale across the cores with torch.distributed (~6 min)

Message: the parallelism is plain torch.distributed and functional collectives, traced into the compiled graphs.

Layout Per DiT block Total
Tensor parallel over 8 cores, CFG as a batch of 2 29.4 ms 13.2 s
CFG-parallel: two groups of 4, one per CFG pass 24.5 ms 11.9 s
+ sequence parallelism (all-gather / reduce-scatter around the matmuls) 21.9 ms 11.1 s
+ cross-attention local to each core's tokens 20.6 ms 10.8 s

models/fast_dit.py#L314-L390

hf = _ag(h)                          # funcol.all_gather_tensor: token shard -> all tokens
q, k, v = _lin(hf, sa.q), _lin(hf, sa.k), _lin(hf, sa.v)
...
y = _rs(_mm(y, sa.o)) + sa.o.bias    # funcol.reduce_scatter_tensor: back to the shard

The VAE is split the same way: each core decodes one spatial tile and rank 0 blends them (VAE 9.0 → 6.0 s). models/vae_tiled.py#L58-L118

7. From benchmark to serving (~8 min)

Message: the compiled model is only useful if the server starts warm, keeps the device fed, and is deployed like any other pod.

Slide: the server

serve_ti2v.py serves the same compiled pipeline the benchmark measures. It runs FastAPI on rank 0 (POST /generate, /health, /readiness), with all 8 ranks in one torchrun. - Fixed shape. Every request image is resized and cropped to the warm-up size, so no request triggers a compile. - Collectives stay on one thread. They must run on the thread that compiled the graphs, so HTTP requests go on a queue and the main thread runs them. - T5 on the CPU, with a prompt cache. It is needed for every request, and it does not fit in HBM next to the DiT and VAE. - Health before readiness. /health answers while the model loads. /readiness turns true only after warm-up.

Slide: warm-up is part of deployment

A lesson from this week: one warm-up run was not enough. On the current image, the second run still traced NKI kernels. The VAE took 186 s, then 21 s, then 3.6 s. Warm up until the timing settles before reporting ready (the server does 3 runs, WARMUP_RUNS).

Slide: keep the device fed

Fixes found as gaps in the system trace: - UniPC scheduler step on the device instead of a round trip to the CPU each step (device busy 96.9% → 99.5%) (device_unipc.py). - Encode the mp4 while the VAE is still decoding, instead of after it. - Start ffmpeg with vfork: forking a process with tens of GB of memory stalled the runtime for 90 ms.

Slide: deploy on EKS

wan2-ti2v-5b-deploy.yaml: a resource claim for the NeuronCores, model weights cached on a PVC, and readiness and liveness probes.

8. Did it stay correct, and where did the time go (~5 min)

Validate every step against the eager reference (scripts/validate/validate_job.sh): - Byte-identical output with the new flags off, and identical output across repeated runs. - Step-0 noise prediction against an fp32 CPU run: within the bf16 floor. - VAE against an exact fp32 decode: 44.6 dB.

Profile with Neuron Explorer: a system trace on every rank shows host gaps, and a device trace on one rank shows the engines, linked back to the source.

The journey:

Stage Total
Eager prototype 76.6 s
+ torch.compile, one graph per block 36.8 s
+ VAE tiled over 8 cores, NKI conv kernels 16.1 s
+ NKI attention, CFG-parallel, sequence parallel 10.8 s
+ VAE fusion, host fixes 8.7 s

For reference, an A100 with torch.compile takes 16.92 s for the same video.

9. Takeaways (~2 min)

  1. Start in eager mode on the neuron device. It gives you a correct baseline with minimal changes.
  2. Compile with torch.compile(backend="neuron"), and choose the scope: one graph per repeated block, with the collectives inside it.
  3. Where one operator dominates, use an NKI kernel from PyTorch. Check its numerics on real data.
  4. Scale with plain torch.distributed and functional collectives.
  5. Serve warm: warm up until the timing settles, gate readiness on it, and keep the host out of the way.
